title: Good Design for Everyone
sub: Grades 5–8 · Art · Motif, pattern and the decorative arts

hero.credit: Court dress, Great Britain, 1860–1865. V&A T.329 to B, AA-1977. © Victoria and Albert Museum, London

objective: The Victoria and Albert Museum was founded in 1852 to show decorative arts and design, to inspire creativity and educate the public: *“a schoolroom for everyone,”* in the words of its first director, Henry Cole. Students will look closely at Victorian design the exhibition shows — a court dress, the museum’s own refreshment room, and two Christmas card borders — and name how each uses **motif**, **repetition**, **symmetry** and **border**. They will design a repeating border of their own for an everyday object, and weigh ornament against function.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: The V&A was founded so that everyone could learn from good design. Every object you use was designed by someone; learning to see those choices lets you make your own.

materials: The pictures on page 3, on screen or printed; the handouts, one per student
Pencils, erasers, rulers; colored pencils and tracing paper if you have them
connection: **Visit the exhibition:** in the *Christmas Card Maker,* try each border — gilt, lace, holly and plain — on the same picture, and decide which suits it best. On poster 1, find the court dress and the V&A’s story.

steps.title: A Chamber of Horrors
script: Ask: *“A museum once opened a gallery of badly designed everyday objects. What would you put in it, and why?”* Take a few answers and ask *why* each time. Then tell students it really happened: the young V&A once had a *“Chamber of Horrors,”* a gallery of badly designed everyday objects, meant to teach visitors good taste. The manufacturers were mortified and complained, and it closed after only two weeks.

screen.question: A museum once opened a gallery of badly designed everyday objects. What would you put in it, and why?

steps.purpose: Start with judgment: what makes a design good or bad?
students: Name one everyday object you think is badly designed.

steps.title: Look closely
script: **Look before naming.** Show the three groups and give students two minutes to point and describe before any words are taught. Then name what they found with the cards below: roses along the dress’s 11-foot train and lace at its edge; the room’s patterned columns, arched stained-glass windows and painted ceiling; the gilt scrolls and scalloped lace of the borders.

**Ornament and function.** Ask what each object is *for*. The dress was worn to be presented at court, where young women practiced for hours to curtsey and walk backward in it; the refreshment room was where visitors ate; a card was sent. Does the ornament help the object do its job, or get in the way?

steps.purpose: Find motif, repetition, symmetry and border in three kinds of Victorian design.
students: Find a motif. Where does it repeat?

steps.title: A schoolroom for everyone
script: **Why a museum?** Gas lighting let the V&A open on winter evenings, so working people could learn from good design too.

screen.cite: Henry Cole, the V&A’s first director

steps.purpose: Connect design to the museum’s purpose: everyone can learn to see it.
students: What could a museum of everyday objects teach?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. Every level ends with a border of the student’s own design for an everyday object.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Finish a mirror-symmetric motif on a grid; continue a border’s repeat; design a border for a card with your own motif.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Find the design choices in two Victorian pieces; try one motif three ways (straight, flipped, mirrored); design a border for an object you choose and explain it.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Critique the four pieces for ornament and function; write design criteria; design a border to meet them; argue whether good design can be taught.

steps.purpose: Design a repeating border at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. Sketch lightly first: designers try many versions.

steps.title: Gallery walk
script: Lay the borders out as a gallery. Partners leave a note on one design: the motif, how it repeats, and whether it suits the object. Close with the hook’s question turned round: *the Chamber of Horrors closed after two weeks. Was it fair to call objects “bad”? Who decides?*

screen.question: Is it well designed? Which choices make you say so?

steps.purpose: Critique each other’s borders kindly, by the criteria.
students: Does it suit the object’s use?

steps.title: Look back
script: Put the objectives back up as *“Can you now…?”* for a thumb up, sideways or down.
